title: (Scenario) Database CPU hits 100% during peak traffic — how do you respond (identify the top CPU-consuming queries first, then look for slow queries, missing indexes, full table scans, inefficient joins, excessive query frequency / N+1 from the app, and connection-pool misconfiguration), and why must you load-test after the fix to confirm it actually helps under realistic traffic?
shortTitle: Database CPU hits 100% during peak traffic — how do you respond

s1_definition.profdef: Responding to database CPU saturation under peak load is a prioritized investigation that starts from the top CPU-consuming queries (via pg_stat_statements or Performance Insights), then diagnoses why each is expensive — missing indexes causing full table scans, inefficient joins, excessive call frequency such as N+1 from the ORM, or connection-pool misconfiguration — and finishes with a load test under realistic traffic to confirm the fix actually holds, because a change that looks good on one query can behave differently under concurrency.
s1_definition.analogy: During salary-day rush, the National Bank's back office machine runs red-hot at 100 percent. You do not panic and buy a bigger machine first. You look at the work log to see which task is eating the most effort — maybe one report is being run ten thousand times because each customer lookup accidentally triggers a fresh search. You fix that one, then you simulate another salary-day rush to make sure the machine stays cool under the real crowd, not just for one quiet test customer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Find the top CPU queries first, fix the biggest offenders, then load-test under realistic peak to prove it actually holds.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Responding to database CPU saturation under peak load is a prioritized investigation that starts from the top CPU-consuming queries (via pg_stat_statements or Performance Insights), then diagnoses why each is expensive — missing indexes causing full table scans, inefficient joins, excessive call frequency such as N+1 from the ORM, or connection-pool misconfiguration — and finishes with a load test under realistic traffic to confirm the fix actually holds, because a change that looks good on one query can behave differently under concurrency.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** During salary-day rush, the National Bank's back office machine runs red-hot at 100 percent. You do not panic and buy a bigger machine first. You look at the work log to see which task is eating the most effort — maybe one report is being run ten thousand times because each customer lookup accidentally triggers a fresh search. You fix that one, then you simulate another salary-day rush to make sure the machine stays cool under the real crowd, not just for one quiet test customer.

**One line to remember:** Find the top CPU queries first, fix the biggest offenders, then load-test under realistic peak to prove it actually holds.

sections.s2_technical:
When database CPU hits 100 percent, resist the urge to scale up immediately. Scaling up hides the real cause and costs money forever. Start by measuring where the CPU goes.

Identify the top CPU-consuming queries. In PostgreSQL, `pg_stat_statements` ranks queries by `total_exec_time` and `calls`. On managed databases, Performance Insights shows the same. The query consuming the most total time is your first target, whether that is because it is individually slow or because it is called a huge number of times.

For each top query, find out why it is expensive. Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and look for a sequential scan on a large table, which means a missing index — the CPU is burning cycles reading every row. Look for inefficient joins such as a nested loop over millions of rows where a hash join would be far cheaper; this usually means a missing index on the join key. Look for sorts spilling to disk.

Look at call frequency, not just per-call cost. A query that takes two milliseconds but runs fifty thousand times per second from an N+1 ORM pattern consumes more total CPU than one slow query. N+1 happens when loading a list of accounts and then firing one extra query per account for its transactions. The fix is a join fetch or batch fetch so one query replaces fifty-one.

Check connection-pool misconfiguration. A pool sized far larger than the database can handle lets too many heavy queries run concurrently, and context switching plus contention drives CPU up. Sometimes a smaller, well-sized pool actually reduces CPU because it limits concurrency to what the database can efficiently handle.

Apply the fix: add the missing index, rewrite the inefficient join, fix the N+1 with a fetch join or batch size, add caching for hot read-mostly queries, and right-size the pool.

Finally, load-test under realistic traffic. This step is non-negotiable because a fix that helps a single query in isolation can behave very differently under concurrency. A new index speeds reads but adds write cost; under a write-heavy peak that trade-off might hurt. Caching helps only if the hit rate is high under real access patterns. A load test with production-like concurrency, data volume, and query mix is the only honest proof that CPU stays healthy at peak. You replay captured traffic or use a tool like k6 or JMeter, watch CPU and P99 latency, and confirm headroom before declaring victory.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — On salary day at the National Bank of India, the database CPU pins at 100 percent and every page slows. This is exactly how CPU saturation behaves — demand exceeds what the current queries can serve efficiently.

Problem 2 — The account dashboard loads a customer's accounts and then, for each account, fires a separate query for its recent transactions. With thousands of customers at peak, this becomes tens of thousands of tiny queries. This is exactly how an N+1 problem drives CPU — many cheap queries add up to enormous total cost.

Problem 3 — After fixing the N+1 with a join fetch, the team declares success on a single-user test. This is exactly why that is premature — only a realistic load test reveals whether CPU stays healthy under the real salary-day crowd.

We will build an `AccountDashboardService` showing the N+1 version and the fixed fetch-join version, a repository with a `@Query` using a join fetch, and a load-test script with k6 that drives realistic concurrency so we can confirm CPU headroom after the fix.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- Enable pg_stat_statements to rank top CPU queries
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;

-- Index on the join key so the transactions fetch uses an index, not a seq scan
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_account ON transactions(account_id);

-- Top CPU-consuming queries (your first investigation step)
SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time, mean_exec_time
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20   # right-sized to DB cores, not arbitrarily huge
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        default_batch_fetch_size: 50   # batches child fetches, kills N+1
        jdbc:
          batch_size: 50
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/dashboard-service-1.0.0.jar

# Step 1: find the top CPU queries
psql bankdb -c "SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time FROM pg_stat_statements \
  ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;"

# Step 2 (MANDATORY): load-test under realistic peak with k6
# test/loadtest/dashboard_peak.js
cat > dashboard_peak.js <<'EOF'
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
export const options = { vus: 200, duration: '2m' };  // 200 concurrent users, 2 min
export default function () {
  const res = http.get('http://localhost:8080/api/v1/dashboard/total');
  check(res, { 'status 200': (r) => r.status === 200, 'p95 < 300ms': (r) => r.timings.duration < 300 });
}
EOF
k6 run dashboard_peak.js

# Step 3: watch DB CPU during the load test (should stay well below 100%)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: salary-day peak traffic, thousands of dashboard requests, each summing transactions across many accounts.

Step 1: Investigation begins. We query `pg_stat_statements` and see that the single highest total-time entry is a tiny transactions-by-account query called fifty thousand times per second. The data tells us the cost is from frequency, not per-call slowness — a classic N+1.

Step 2: We confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the per-call query is fine individually but that there is no index on the join key, so each call does extra work. We add `idx_txn_account`.

Step 3: We change the repository to `findAllWithTransactions`, which issues one join-fetch query instead of one-plus-N. In the data path, fifty-one queries collapse into one.

Step 4: The service sums all transactions from the single result set. Total CPU for this endpoint drops sharply because the database runs one efficient join instead of tens of thousands of tiny lookups.

Step 5: The mandatory load test runs. We drive two hundred concurrent virtual users for two minutes with k6. The data here is realistic concurrency, not a single request. We watch database CPU and P95 latency.

Step 6: CPU now peaks around sixty percent with P95 under three hundred milliseconds, giving headroom. Only now do we declare the fix successful, because it held under realistic traffic rather than for one isolated query.

```
2026-10-25 13:50:30 INFO  AccountDashboardService - Summed 5000 accounts with a single fetch-join query
k6: http_req_duration p(95)=214ms  checks=100%  db_cpu_peak=61%
```

```
  Only after load test passes → declare fix successful
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When database CPU hits one hundred percent at peak, my first move is never to scale up the machine, because that hides the real cause and costs money forever. I start by identifying the top CPU-consuming queries using pg_stat_statements or Performance Insights, ranked by total execution time and by call count, because the biggest offender is often not one slow query but a cheap query called tens of thousands of times.

For each top query I run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to understand why it is expensive. A sequential scan on a large table means a missing index. A nested loop over millions of rows means a missing index on a join key where a hash join would be far cheaper. A tiny query with a massive call count almost always means an N+1 pattern from the ORM, where loading a list then triggers one extra query per element. I also check the connection pool, because a pool sized far larger than the database can handle lets too many heavy queries run at once and actually raises CPU through contention.

I then apply the targeted fix: add the missing index, rewrite the inefficient join, replace N+1 with a fetch join or batch fetch so fifty-one queries become one, cache hot read-mostly results, and right-size the pool to the database's capacity rather than making it arbitrarily large.

The step I never skip is load testing under realistic traffic after the fix, and I always explain why: a change that looks great on a single query in isolation can behave completely differently under concurrency. A new index speeds reads but adds write cost, which can hurt during a write-heavy peak, and caching only helps if the hit rate is high under real access patterns. At the National Bank of India our salary-day dashboard pinned the database at one hundred percent because each request fired one query per account in an N+1 loop. I added an index on the join key and switched to a single fetch-join query, then I replayed salary-day concurrency with k6 at two hundred virtual users. CPU dropped to around sixty percent with P95 latency under three hundred milliseconds, and only then did I call it fixed — because the load test, not a single quiet query, is the honest proof that it holds under the real crowd.
